title: Systemic disease
description: Oral and dental manifestations of systemic disease — the moment when a routine dental exam picks up an undiagnosed haematological, endocrine, autoimmune, or metabolic condition.

problems.description: Gums swell and bleed spontaneously, with petechial spots on the palate and mucosal pallor; candidosis or herpetic ulcers arise without obvious local cause.
problems.etiology: What happens is a neoplastic white cell proliferation floods the peripheral blood with primitive blast cells [2]. The result is reduced resistance to infection and bleeding problems — those two failures are what you see in the mouth [1]. The leukaemia split matters clinically: acute myeloid is the adult version, acute lymphoblastic is the childhood one, and the latter now carries up to 90% cure rate in favourable cases [2].
problems.presentation: Gingival swelling and hypertrophy come first, then spontaneous bleeding — not just on probing, but unprovoked [1]. Petechial haemorrhages dot the palate and buccal mucosa with minimal or no trauma [1]. Mucosal pallor reflects the underlying anaemia. The interesting bit is that candida and herpes can follow because resistance to infection has collapsed [1]. So when you see a cluster of gingival swelling, spontaneous bleeding, and opportunistic oral infections without any local periodontal explanation — the dental chair may be where this diagnosis first surfaces, before any systemic workup.
problems.results: While awaiting haematological management, spontaneous gingival bleeding can be controlled by using impressions as a made-to-measure pressure dressing [3] — a practical local measure that buys time without causing harm.
problems.definingCharacteristics: The defining cluster is spontaneous gingival bleeding, gingival swelling, mucosal pallor, and opportunistic oral infections — all arriving together, with no local periodontal explanation to account for them. Petechial haemorrhages on the palate with minimal trauma are particularly significant [1]. Individually these signs appear in other conditions; the combination without a local cause is what flags the systemic differential.
problems.treatment: Recognise it and refer same-day — that's the GDP's job here. Locally: improve oral hygiene, avoid extractions, use local haemostatic methods [3]. Start chlorhexidine mouthwashes to head off superinfection; treat any infections that do arise aggressively [3]. Avoid aspirin, other NSAIDs, trauma, and IM injections [4]. The impression-as-pressure-dressing trick [3] is worth remembering for controlling spontaneous ooze while you arrange the urgent referral.
problems.prognosis: Outcome depends entirely on leukaemia type and stage at diagnosis. Acute lymphoblastic leukaemia in children reaches up to 90% cure rate in favourable cases; acute myeloid in adults achieves high remission rates but tends to relapse [2]. The takeaway: early detection improves outcome, and oral signs can be the first clue.

citations.quote: This and other haematological malignancies are associated with a ↓ in resistance to infection leading to candidosis or herpetic infections. Other oral problems include bleeding and petechial haemorrhage (even with minimal trauma), gingival swelling, ulceration, and mucosal pallor.

A neoplastic proliferation of white blood cells. Acute leukaemias are characterized by the release of primitive blast cells into the peripheral blood and account for 50% of childhood malignancy. Acute lymphoblastic leukaemia, the commonest childhood leukaemia, now has up to 90% cure rate in favourable cases. May present as gingival hypertrophy and bleeding. Acute myeloid leukaemia is the commonest acute leukaemia of adults, with high remission rates possible but a tendency to relapse.

Prevention of superinfection with chlorhexidine mouthwashes and aggressive appropriate Rx of infections which arise are of real help. Management of the bleeding is aimed at the underlying disorder; local techniques include improving OH, avoiding extractions, and using local haemostatic methods. Spontaneous gingival bleeding may be controlled by using impressions as a made-to-measure pressure dressing.

In haematological malignancy, anaemia, bleeding, and infection are the overwhelming risks. Look for and treat anaemia. Avoid aspirin, other NSAIDs, trauma, and IM injections. Prevent sepsis, and if it occurs, treat very aggressively with the locally recommended broad-spectrum antibacterials and antifungals.

problems.description: Sore, atrophic tongue, angular cheilitis, and recurrent mouth ulcers in a patient with no obvious local cause; burning mouth without mucosal change may be the presenting sign.
problems.conditionName: Iron, B12, or folate deficiency — oral manifestations
problems.etiology: Iron, B12, and folate deficiencies are all associated with oral mucosal problems [1]. The reason this matters to a GDP is that the oral signs can appear before a frank anaemia shows up on a blood count [1]. Deficiency is present; haemoglobin hasn't dropped enough to flag it yet. B12 drops in pernicious anaemia, alcohol abuse, small gut disease, or chronic nitrous oxide exposure [4]. Low folate is mostly dietary, though illness and certain drugs can also reduce it [4].
problems.presentation: Atrophic glossitis — smooth, sore, depapillated tongue — is the classic picture [1]. Red lines or patches on a sore but visually unremarkable tongue lean toward B12 [1]. Recurrent aphthous ulcers are associated with all three deficiencies [1]. Angular cheilitis fits iron deficiency and general anaemia [3]. The sore, clinically normal tongue — burning tongue — is sometimes the earliest sign, appearing even before anaemia is confirmed biochemically [1]. Oral candida can be precipitated or worsened by iron deficiency specifically [1].
problems.results: Clinically, look for pallor of the conjunctivae and palmar creases, brittle or spoon-shaped nails — these systemic signs sit alongside the oral ones [3]. In all cases the cause must be sought, which may necessitate referral to a haematologist [2].
problems.definingCharacteristics: Oral signs appearing without local mucosal disease, in the context of haematinic deficiency — that's the defining pattern. The triad of sore atrophic tongue, angular cheilitis, and recurrent aphthae, particularly in a young or middle-aged woman, is the classic cluster. The less-recognised feature: burning mouth without any mucosal change as a precursor of anaemia [1]. It's the oral sign you can easily attribute to stress or habit until bloods prove otherwise.
problems.treatment: Request haematinic bloods and refer to the GP or haematologist for cause investigation and correction [2]. The GP prescribes: ferrous sulfate 200 mg three times daily for iron; lifelong IM hydroxocobalamin 1 mg 3-monthly for B12; folic acid 5 mg daily for folate [2]. The goal is to find and fix the cause — treat the mouth symptomatically in the meantime.
problems.prognosis: Oral signs resolve once the deficiency is corrected. Pernicious anaemia means lifelong B12 replacement [2].

citations.quote: The nutritional deficiencies associated with anaemia, iron, vitamin B12, and folate, are all associated with recurrent oral ulceration and specific deficiencies may be present, even in the absence of a frank anaemia. Atrophic glossitis was formerly the commonest oral symptom of anaemia but is less often seen now. Red lines or patches on a sore, but normal-looking tongue may indicate vitamin B12 deficiency. Candidosis may be precipitated or exacerbated by anaemia, particularly iron deficiency, and angular cheilitis is a well-recognized association. The sore, clinically normal tongue (burning tongue) is sometimes a manifestation or even precursor of anaemia.

In all cases the cause must be sought; this may necessitate referral to a haematologist. Drugs used in iron deficiency: ferrous sulfate 200mg tds. Lifelong IM hydroxocobalamin 1mg 3-monthly is used to treat vitamin B12 deficiency, and folic acid 5mg od for folate deficiency.

These are notoriously unreliable, but may include general fatigue, heart failure, angina on effort, pallor (look at conjunctivae and palmar creases, but unreliable), brittle nails &/or spoon-shaped nails (koilonychia), oral discomfort &/or ulceration, glossitis, and classically angular cheilitis.

Vitamin B12 is ↓ in pernicious anaemia (deficit of intrinsic factor), alcohol abuse, small gut disease, and chronic exposure to nitrous oxide. Low folate is usually dietary, but may be caused by illness (e.g. coeliac disease, skin disease) or drugs such as phenytoin, methotrexate, trimethoprim, and co-trimoxazole.

problems.description: Severe or rapidly progressive periodontal disease, dry mouth, and oral thrush in a patient whose glycaemic control is poor; burning mouth or slow healing after extractions may accompany these signs.
problems.etiology: Persistent hyperglycaemia [2] leads to reduced resistance to infection when control is poor [1]. In poorly controlled diabetes this drives accelerated periodontal disease and repeated oral candida. Peripheral neuropathy can present as burning mouth or facial dysaesthesia [1]. Sialosis appears as a late feature [1].
problems.presentation: Severe periodontal disease that's out of proportion to the patient's plaque control is the most important red flag [1]. Xerostomia compounds this by stripping away salivary protection [1]. Oral candida — including angular cheilitis — follows the compromised immune response [1]. Slow or incomplete healing after extractions or minor oral surgery is a consistent pattern [1]. Burning mouth or facial dysaesthesia in a patient with no mucosal cause raises peripheral neuropathy as a differential [1]. Lichenoid reactions on the buccal mucosa can also arise from oral hypoglycaemic drugs [1].
problems.results: No single oral sign is pathognomonic. When these features cluster without a local explanation, screen for diabetes.
problems.definingCharacteristics: Accelerated periodontal breakdown in a patient who seems to be maintaining their plaque control reasonably well — that's the clue worth noticing. Pair it with xerostomia and recurrent candida and the picture becomes hard to ignore. Bilateral parotid swelling of sialosis, when it appears as a late finding, is a visible marker. Oral burning or dysaesthesia without a mucosal cause in an older patient should put undiagnosed diabetes on the differential list.
problems.treatment: Recognise it and refer to the GP for glycaemic screening. Plan any oral surgery carefully; there is a tendency to slower healing following surgery [1]. If you're seeing lichenoid drug reactions, talk to the prescribing physician about alternative hypoglycaemics [1].
problems.prognosis: Oral complications track glycaemic control closely [1].

citations.quote: No specific oral changes, although manifestations of ↓ resistance to infection can be seen if poorly controlled (e.g. severe periodontal disease). Xerostomia and thrush are prominent features of ketoacidosis. Sialosis is sometimes seen as a late feature of diabetes. Burning mouth may be a presenting feature, and oral or facial dysaesthesia may reflect the peripheral neuropathies seen in diabetics. There is a tendency to slower healing following surgery. Lichenoid reactions due to oral hypoglycaemic drugs may be seen.
Persistent hyperglycaemia due to a relative deficiency of insulin.

problems.description: Loss of lamina dura on dental radiographs, ground-glass bone pattern in the jaws, or a multilocular cystic jaw lesion found incidentally on routine radiography.
problems.conditionName: Hyperparathyroidism — jaw lesions and lamina dura loss
problems.etiology: Primary hyperparathyroidism comes from hyperplasia or adenoma of the parathyroid glands [1]. The mechanism: raised PTH mobilises calcium out of bone, raising plasma Ca²⁺ [1]. Secondary hyperparathyroidism is the body's response to low plasma calcium — for example, in renal failure. Tertiary follows when the parathyroids keep overproducing even after calcium has been normalised [2]. The reason early detection matters: irreversible renal damage occurs without treatment [1].
problems.presentation: In the jaws, this is primarily a radiographic story. What you'll see: loss of the lamina dura around teeth, a generalised ground-glass trabecular pattern replacing normal bone architecture, and cystic radiolucent lesions that often appear multilocular [1]. The cysts contain dark-coloured tissue — histologically identical to giant cell granuloma, which is why they're called brown tumours [1]. The jaw radiograph is often where the condition surfaces first, ahead of any systemic symptoms the patient might report.
problems.results: Biochemistry confirms the diagnosis: raised serum calcium, raised PTH, lowered alkaline phosphatase [1]. The combination of raised Ca²⁺ and raised PTH is the diagnostic pair [1]. Here's the important thing about biopsy: the brown tumour is histologically indistinguishable from giant cell granuloma on tissue alone — you need the systemic biochemistry to tell them apart [1].
problems.definingCharacteristics: Loss of lamina dura on its own isn't specific to hyperparathyroidism. But pair it with a ground-glass jaw pattern and a multilocular giant-cell lesion — especially in a patient with unexplained renal impairment — and you have the radiographic triad. Bilateral or multi-site brown tumours are strongly suggestive. It's rare, but worth catching: untreated, irreversible renal damage is the consequence [1].
problems.treatment: Recognise the radiographic pattern and refer urgently for medical investigation. Any jaw lesion fitting this picture — multilocular radiolucency, ground-glass bone, loss of lamina dura — without a prior local explanation warrants blood calcium and PTH measurement. Surgical management of the parathyroid lesion is the physician's territory.
problems.prognosis: With early treatment, prognosis is good. The main risk is delayed diagnosis and the irreversible renal damage that follows [1]. Brown tumours regress once hyperparathyroidism is corrected.

citations.quote: Rare. Caused by hyperplasia or adenoma of the parathyroids. ↑ parathormone causes ↑ plasma Ca2+ liberated from bone. Irreversible renal damage in absence of Rx so worth detecting (diagnosis confirmed by ↑ Ca2+, ↑ PTH, ↓ alkaline phosphatase). Appears in the jaws as loss of lamina dura; a 'ground-glass' appearance of bone and cystic lesions (often looking multilocular), which contain dark-coloured tissue; 'brown tumour' histologically indistinguishable from a giant cell granuloma.
1° is caused by an adenoma. 2° is a response to low plasma Ca2+, e.g. in renal failure, and 3° follows on from 2° when the parathyroids continue ↑ production, even if Ca2+ is normalized.

problems.description: Persistent linear oral ulcers, cobblestoning of the buccal mucosa with mucosal tags, or diffuse lip swelling without obvious local cause; oral features may predate gut symptoms.
problems.etiology: Crohn's is a chronic granulomatous disease of unknown cause — it can affect any part of the gut from mouth to anus [1]. About 1% of cases present with oral ulceration before any gut symptoms appear, which means the GDP is sometimes first on the scene [1]. Orofacial granulomatosis is probably a variant of the same process — a hypersensitivity response to certain foods or additives, particularly benzoates [2].
problems.presentation: The oral lesions affect gingiva, buccal mucosa, and lips [1]. What you'll typically find: purplish-red non-haemorrhagic swellings, linear long-standing ulcers — not the round punched-out morphology of common aphthae — cobblestoning of the buccal mucosa, and mucosal tags and folds [1]. Lip swelling from granulomatous cheilitis can be striking and visible across the room. These features can appear years before the patient develops any gastrointestinal symptoms, so you may be diagnosing Crohn's without the patient having any gut complaints at all [1].
problems.results: The key histological finding is non-caseating granulomata on biopsy [2]. Biopsy alone confirms the tissue diagnosis; gastrointestinal investigations are then needed to establish gut involvement.
problems.definingCharacteristics: Linear, persistent, non-healing ulcers combined with cobblestone mucosal texture and mucosal tags are the hallmark [1]. Add lip swelling with an orofacial granulomatosis pattern and suspicion climbs further. The distinction from common aphthous ulcers is in the linearity, the persistence, and the cobblestone surface of the surrounding mucosa [1].
problems.treatment: Recognise the pattern and refer to gastroenterology or general medicine. For the oral lesions: topical steroids or simple excision work well for pain relief [1], but the goal is to treat the systemic disease. For orofacial granulomatosis specifically, identifying and avoiding irritant dietary factors — particularly benzoates — is the most effective approach [2]. Severe or refractory cases may need systemic therapy: sulfasalazine or infliximab [2]. Don't manage these lesions in isolation; medical coordination is essential.
problems.prognosis: Oral manifestations tend to track gut disease activity. When intestinal Crohn's is controlled, oral signs often improve. Some oral lesions persist independently. The interesting thing about orofacial granulomatosis without confirmed gut disease: dietary modification alone can sometimes control it fully [2].

citations.quote: Chronic granulomatous disease of unknown aetiology affecting any part of the gut from mouth to anus. Primarily affects the terminal third of the ileum, although ~1% of cases will present with oral ulceration predating any other symptoms. These tend to affect the gingiva, buccal mucosa, and lips with purplish-red non-haemorrhagic swellings, linear long-standing ulcers and cobblestoning of buccal mucosa with mucosal tags and folds. Orofacial granulomatosis is probably a variant. Painful oral lesions seem to respond well to topical steroids or simple excision but Rx is aimed at the systemic disease.

This is clinically and histologically identical to oral manifestations of Crohn's disease. ∆ of exclusion (Crohn's, sarcoid). Probable aetiology is as a hypersensitivity response to certain foods, additives such as benzoates, etc. ∆ is biopsy to demonstrate granulomata histologically and exclusion of systemic disease. Most beneficial Rx is to identify and avoid the irritant factors. Patients who have generalized Crohn's or very severe orofacial granulomatosis may benefit from systemic Rx with sulfasalazine or infliximab.

Crohn's disease may affect any part of the gastrointestinal tract but has a preference for the ileo-caecal area. It is a chronic granulomatous disease affecting the full thickness of the mucosa and may result in fistula formation.

problems.description: Wound oozing restarts an hour or more after extraction, continuing as a slow intractable bleed after the initial clot appeared to form normally.
problems.etiology: Haemophilia A is an X-linked recessive deficiency of factor VIII — it affects males predominantly, though female haemophiliacs can occur [1]. All daughters of affected males are potential carriers [1]. The severity of any bleed depends on two things: the level of residual factor VIII activity, and the degree of trauma [1]. Haemophilia B — factor IX deficiency, Christmas disease — is clinically identical in presentation [2].
problems.presentation: Oral bleeding is common in haemophilia [1]. The characteristic pattern is deceptive: following trauma, bleeding appears to stop as the platelet plug forms normally, then an intractable general ooze restarts after an hour or so [1]. This is the thing to grasp — it's not an immediate gush. The initial haemostasis looks fine. The delayed-onset ooze is what catches people out, because by the time it starts the patient may be at home. Haemarthroses are the more common systemic presentation and typically surface in childhood [1].
problems.results: In practice, most patients with haemophilia A will tell you on their medical history form. The GDP scenario where this surfaces as a surprise is an unexplained prolonged post-extraction ooze in a case not previously recognised [1].
problems.definingCharacteristics: The one-hour delay before the ooze restarts is the pathognomonic behavioural pattern [1]. The absence of a local cause for prolonged bleeding, combined with a history of childhood haemarthroses, points directly to the diagnosis [1].
problems.treatment: Always manage haemophilia patients through specialist centres. Check the patient's warning card for the specialist contact number [3] — that call happens before you do anything. If you're dealing with an active bleed, local measures, tranexamic acid, and platelet transfusion are the tools available [4].
problems.prognosis: Haemophilia patients should always be managed through specialist centres [3]. Proceed with any dental procedure only after specialist clearance.

citations.quote: The commonest clotting defect. Inherited as a sex-linked recessive, it affects males predominantly, although female haemophiliacs can occur. All daughters of affected males are potential carriers. Usually presents in childhood as haemarthroses. Bleeding from the mouth is common. Following trauma, bleeding appears to stop, but an intractable general ooze starts after an hour or so. Severity of bleeding is dependent on the level of factor VIII activity and degree of trauma.
Clinically identical to haemophilia A; also known as Christmas disease.
The haemophilias and Von Willebrand's disease should always be managed at specialist centres. Check the patient's warning card for the contact telephone number.
If actively bleeding, use a combination of local measures, tranexamic acid, and platelet transfusion.
